analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: The FAMILY Act, introduced in May 2023 with 36 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a national paid family and medical leave insurance program run out of the Social Security Administration. Workers who need leave for a new child, a serious health condition, care for a family member, or safety from domestic violence could draw up to 60 days of benefits a year, with lower-paid workers replacing up to 85% of their wages (between $580 and $4,000 a month, adjusted over time). It would be funded by a 0.2% payroll tax on both employees and employers (0.4% on self-employment income), and states that already run paid leave programs would be reimbursed for the benefits they pay. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need time off for the birth or adoption of a child, their own serious health condition, care for a spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, or chosen family member, or safety-related leave after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. The program covers self-employed workers and does not require a minimum workweek, only about $2,000 of recent earnings, so part-time and gig-adjacent workers can qualify. Lower-wage workers benefit most: the benefit replaces 85% of earnings up to a threshold, versus 50% at higher incomes, and every claim carries a floor of $580 a month. The bill also bars employers from firing, demoting, or retaliating against workers who take the leave, requires restoring them to the same or an equivalent job, and requires keeping their health coverage active during leave. States that already run paid leave programs (California, New Jersey, New York, and others) would receive federal grants covering most of their benefit costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid leave, especially lower-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federally guaranteed paid leave benefit of up to 60 caregiving days per 12-month benefit period (no more than 20 days in a month) for a worker's own serious health condition, care for a broad list of family members, or safety-related leave after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Replaces 85% of average monthly earnings for the lowest earners, 69% for middle ranges, and 50% above that, with a monthly minimum of $580 and maximum of $4,000, both indexed to wage growth, so the benefit is most generous relative to pay for the lowest-wage workers.

Covers self-employed workers and requires only about $2,000 in recent wages or self-employment income to qualify, with applications allowed retroactively up to 90 days after leave begins, which opens the program to part-time and irregular workers.

Makes it unlawful for an employer to fire, demote, discriminate against, or retaliate against a worker for taking the leave, requires reinstatement to the same or an equivalent position, requires health coverage to be maintained during leave, and creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation for adverse actions within 12 months of leave, enforceable in court with attorney's fees.

Funds the benefit through a dedicated trust fund financed by a 0.2% payroll tax on employees and 0.2% on employers (0.4% on self-employment income), explicitly separate from the Social Security trust fund, and reimburses states with existing paid leave programs for their benefit costs.

analysis.who_pays: Employees and employers each pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on all covered wages, and self-employed people pay 0.4% on net self-employment income, starting 120 days after enactment — the standard economic caveat is that the employer half tends to be passed to workers over time through slower wage growth. Employers also bear the operational cost of holding a job open, restoring the worker to the same or an equivalent position, and maintaining health coverage during leave, and face court-enforceable liability, including doubled liquidated damages and attorney's fees, if they retaliate. Federal taxpayers front the start-up administrative costs, which the bill requires be repaid to the Treasury within 10 years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employees and employers through a new payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The program is paid for by a tax on every covered worker, so the majority of workers in any given year who take no leave still pay into it; and because employers pay a matching 0.2%, part of the cost is likely to show up as slower wage growth for those same workers.

Benefits are capped at 60 caregiving days per 12-month benefit period and 20 days in any month, so a worker facing a long recovery, a premature birth, or extended elder care would exhaust the benefit well before the situation ends — much shorter than the leave many other developed countries provide.

Employers of every size face new obligations: paying the tax, restoring workers to equivalent positions, maintaining health coverage during leave, and potentially defending retaliation lawsuits that carry doubled damages and attorney's fees for workers who prevail.

The new Office of Paid Family and Medical Leave within the Social Security Administration would determine eligibility, verify medical certifications, and process monthly claims, an administrative build-out with fraud-prevention and adjudication duties that would take years and start-up appropriations to stand up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is substantial: paid leave is currently available to only a minority of American workers, and this program would cover virtually all of them, with the most generous replacement rates going to the lowest-paid. The cost is real but modest by the standards of social insurance: a combined 0.4% payroll tax split between workers and employers, a strict 60-day annual cap that limits total spending, and start-up costs that must be repaid to the Treasury within a decade. The main design trade-off is that the cap keeps the program affordable but leaves workers facing long illnesses or extended caregiving stretches without income after two months. The bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh these trade-offs in any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or a vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the FAMILY Act on May 18, 2023, with 31 original cosponsors, all Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over payroll taxes and Social Security, on the day of introduction.

Over the remaining roughly 19 months of the 118th Congress, the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill was never brought to the Senate floor. That is the last entry in its official action history.
By the end of the Congress the bill had 36 cosponsors (35 Democrats and 1 Independent) and no Republican support; no version ever passed either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the new payroll tax and held jobs and health coverage open during leave are better off because the bill died, as are businesses that currently provide no paid leave and would have faced new obligations. Workers who needed paid leave — especially low-wage workers and new parents without employer benefits — gained nothing, because the program never came into existence.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the new tax and leave mandates

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and recruited a broad slate of Democratic cosponsors; has carried versions of this bill for roughly a decade.

for.name: 36 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Democratic senators plus Independent Bernie Sanders, including Chuck Schumer, Patty Murray, Sherrod Brown-era colleagues, Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Ron Wyden-era committee members such as Ben Cardin and Tom Carper
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a majority-sized Democratic roster in the Senate, though none of them moved it out of committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 18, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Not one of the bill's 36 cosponsors was a Republican, and the bill never attracted Republican support in the Finance Committee or on the floor; several prior versions of the FAMILY Act likewise drew opposition over the payroll tax and employer mandates.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 36 cosponsors was a Democrat or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and because the bill never reached a hearing or floor vote, the partisan split was never tested with a roll call.

industries.note: Every covered employer would pay a 0.2% payroll tax, hold jobs open, restore workers to equivalent positions, maintain their health coverage during leave, and face court-enforceable penalties for retaliation. Employers that currently offer no paid leave would lose the ability to compete for workers without it.

industries.industry: Paid-leave insurers and benefit plan administrators
industries.note: In states with existing paid leave programs, benefits delivered through employer contracts with insurers would be reimbursed with federal grant money, routing public funds through those insurers. Insurers operating only in states without programs gain no new mandate-based market, unlike state-model bills that create one everywhere.

industries.industry: Workers in high-turnover, low-wage industries (retail, food service, care work)
industries.note: These are the industries where paid leave is least commonly offered; the bill's low earnings threshold ($2,000 over recent quarters) and high replacement rate (85%) are designed to reach exactly these workers.
